back2basics.text: Judicial discretion allows courts to decide appropriate sentences based on case facts within legal limits. Due process ensures fair legal procedures before depriving a person of life or liberty, protecting constitutional rights.

2026-11-05-am-37e758cc0c.deck: The Supreme Court upheld the death penalty in 1980 but established judicial guidelines to ensure careful discretion in sentencing. These safeguards remain relevant for understanding judicial processes and human rights in capital punishment.

body.label: Upholding death penalty
body.text: In Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the death penalty but imposed conditions for its application.

body.label: Judicial discretion guidelines

body.label: Legislative alignment
body.text: The Court followed the legislative scheme under Section 354(3) of the CrPC (now Section 393(3) of BNSS, 2023), which makes life imprisonment the norm and death penalty exceptional.

back2basics.text: Biodiversity conservation involves protecting species, habitats, and ecosystems to maintain ecological balance. Protected areas are legally designated regions like national parks and wildlife sanctuaries that conserve biodiversity. Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (OECMs) are sites outside these protected areas that also contribute to biodiversity conservation through effective management and governance.

2026-11-05-am-51f105fdfa.deck: The Union Environment Minister released the Guidelines for Designation of India’s Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (I-OECMs) 2026 at CBD COP-17 in Armenia. These guidelines establish a framework to recognize areas outside legally protected zones that contribute to long-term biodiversity conservation, supporting India's international biodiversity commitments.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about India’s Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (I-OECMs):
1. I-OECMs are legally protected areas managed only by the Central Government.
2. The GEF-8 project supporting I-OECMs aims to add 3% of India’s land and marine area to the conservation estate beyond the existing 27% under protection.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.trap: Statement 1 is incorrect because I-OECMs are areas outside legally protected areas and can be managed by Central or State Governments or government-recognised local institutions, not only by the Central Government.

body.label: Definition
body.text: I-OECMs are areas outside legally protected zones that deliver positive and sustained long-term outcomes for in-situ biodiversity conservation through effective management.

body.label: Scope of ecosystems
body.text: The guidelines cover terrestrial, inland water, coastal, and marine ecosystems including biodiversity parks, sacred groves, community-managed irrigation tanks, seagrass and seaweed beds, and fisheries seasonal ban areas.

body.label: Recognition criteria
body.text: Four mandatory criteria include: the area must not be legally protected, must be governed under government or government-recognised local institutions, have defined boundaries without overlap with protected areas, and recognition must not alter existing governance or activities.

sections.heading: What are India’s Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (I-OECMs)?

body.label: Application process
body.text: Applications can be submitted to the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) by government departments, local self-governments, and Biodiversity Management Committees.

body.label: Validation and approval
body.text: NBA conducts preliminary examination, forwards applications to State Biodiversity Boards or Union Territory Biodiversity Councils for validation, and makes final decisions with MoEFCC coordination.

body.label: Monitoring framework
body.text: Each recognized site must have measurable indicators assessed at least every five years, with records maintained by State Biodiversity Boards or UT Biodiversity Councils.

body.label: Publication and capacity building
body.text: MoEFCC and NBA will liaise with UNEP-WCMC to publish recognized sites on the World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas, and provide capacity-building and non-monetary recognition for good practices.

sections.heading: How are I-OECMs designated and managed?

body.label: Support to global targets
body.text: I-OECMs support India’s implementation of Target 3 (30x30) of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and National Biodiversity Target 3 under the updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (2024–2030).

body.label: Conservation beyond protected areas
body.text: They enable conservation of biodiversity through effective management outside legally protected areas, expanding the conservation estate.

body.label: Complementary government project
body.text: A GEF-8 project aims to implement the guidelines in six demonstration sites, adding 3% of India’s land and marine area to conservation estates beyond the existing 27% under protection.

sections.heading: Why do I-OECMs matter for India’s biodiversity commitments?

body.label: Project duration and financing
body.text: The project runs for 72 months from 15 May 2026 to 15 May 2032, with total financing of USD 60.79 million including a GEF Trust Fund grant of USD 6.65 million.

body.label: Project goals
body.text: It aims to establish 50,000 hectares of new terrestrial conservation areas, restore at least 5,000 hectares of degraded land, and directly benefit at least 50,000 people, half of them women.

body.label: Demonstration sites
body.text: Sites include the Gori Valley (Uttarakhand), Kumbhalgarh–Mount Abu–Jaisalmer (Rajasthan), Satkosia–Kalahandi (Odisha), Srisailam–Cumbum (Andhra Pradesh and Telangana), Sahyadri–Konkan (Maharashtra and Goa), and Lakshadweep Islands Marinescape.

body.label: Project components
body.text: The project focuses on enabling frameworks, financing and capacity building, increased coverage and management effectiveness, knowledge management, and monitoring and evaluation.

back2basics.text: Reservation of constituencies is a constitutional mechanism to ensure representation of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in legislative bodies. Reserved constituencies are identified based on the proportion of SC/ST population in an area. Rotation of reserved seats means periodically changing which constituencies are reserved to prevent permanent reservation of the same seats. However, the current legal framework does not mandate rotation for Parliament and State Assemblies, unlike local bodies where rotation is provided under specific constitutional provisions.

2026-11-05-am-5d8979901d.deck: The Supreme Court refused to order rotation of constituencies reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Parliament and State Assemblies, ruling this is a legislative matter. This ruling clarifies the judiciary's role in reservation policies and electoral laws, relevant for constitutional and governance studies.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements regarding SC/ST reserved constituencies in Parliament and State Assemblies:
1. The Supreme Court has mandated rotation of reserved constituencies to ensure fairness.
2. The identification of reserved constituencies is based on the proportion of SC/ST population as per the Delimitation Act, 2002.

mcq.trap: Statement 1 is incorrect because the Supreme Court refused to mandate rotation, stating it is a legislative matter.

body.label: No court-ordered rotation
body.text: The Supreme Court held that the rotation of SC/ST reserved constituencies in Parliament and State Assemblies is a matter for the legislature and cannot be directed by the judiciary.

body.label: Upholding Delimitation Act
body.text: The Court refused to interfere with the Allahabad High Court's judgment upholding Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, 2002, which identifies reserved constituencies based on higher SC/ST population concentrations.

sections.heading: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding rotation of reserved seats?

body.label: Petitioner's claim
body.text: The petitioner challenged the continued reservation of a constituency for nearly seven decades, arguing that absence of rotation violated Articles 14, 15, and 19 of the Constitution and limited voter choice.

body.label: Court's reasoning
body.text: The Court noted that voters in a multiparty democracy vote based on political ideologies rather than caste, and that candidates from the general category can contest non-reserved seats, distinguishing voting rights from contesting rights.

body.label: Forum for change
body.text: Chief Justice Surya Kant remarked that the petitioner approached the wrong forum and suggested taking the issue to Parliament or through public protests.

sections.heading: What were the petitioner's arguments and the Court's response?

body.label: Legislature's domain
body.text: The ruling affirms that decisions on reservation seat rotation fall within the legislative domain, reinforcing separation of powers.

body.label: Clarifies reservation policy
body.text: It clarifies that the current reservation system for SC/ST constituencies is based on demographic concentration rather than rotation, impacting electoral representation.

body.label: Implications for electoral choices
body.text: The judgment highlights the balance between protecting reserved constituencies and ensuring voter choice within constitutional limits.

sections.heading: Why does this ruling matter for constitutional law and governance?

back2basics.text: The Drugs Rules, 1945, regulate the manufacture, sale, and distribution of drugs in India. Manufacturing licences are granted under these rules and can be suspended or cancelled for non-compliance. Currently, suspension requires a show-cause notice, which can delay action against substandard drugs. The regulatory framework aims to ensure drug safety, efficacy, and quality to protect public health.

2026-11-05-am-b3213cd55d.deck: The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to allow immediate suspension of manufacturing licences for drugs found Not of Standard Quality (NSQ) on critical parameters. This aims to strengthen regulatory oversight, ensure patient safety, and improve accountability in drug manufacturing.

body.label: Immediate suspension provision
body.text: The Ministry proposes immediate suspension of manufacturing licences for drugs declared NSQ on critical parameters like Assay, Dissolution, Related Substances, Impurities, or Sterility, bypassing the earlier procedural delay.

body.label: Corrective action before revocation
body.text: Suspended licences can be restored only after manufacturers conduct root cause analysis and implement corrective and preventive actions (CAPA) verified by the licensing authority.

body.label: Enhanced reporting mechanism
body.text: Government Analyst reports will be simultaneously sent to the Drugs Controller General of India, State/UT Licensing Authority, manufacturer, and marketer to ensure coordinated regulatory action.

body.text: Previously, suspension required a show-cause notice causing delays during which substandard drugs could remain in circulation, posing risks to public health.

body.label: Protecting patient safety
body.text: Prompt suspension on key quality failures reduces potential harm from unsafe medicines and facilitates effective recall.

body.label: Strengthening accountability
body.text: The new mechanism promotes greater responsibility among manufacturers and marketers by ensuring timely regulatory intervention and follow-up.

sections.heading: Why is immediate suspension of licences important for drug regulation?

back2basics.text: Fast Track Courts are special courts set up to expedite the trial and disposal of cases that require urgent attention, such as sexual offences. They aim to reduce pendency and deliver timely justice by dedicating judicial and prosecutorial resources exclusively to these cases. The scheme is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, meaning funding is shared between the central government and states/UTs.

2026-11-05-am-c26d9bde5a.deck: The Union Cabinet approved the continuation of the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Fast Track Special Courts (FTSCs) for rape and POCSO cases for five more years from 2026-27 to 2030-31. This scheme aims to expedite trials, reduce case backlogs, and provide victim-friendly court environments, which is crucial for justice delivery in sexual offence cases.

body.label: Scheme purpose
body.text: The scheme provides dedicated courts for speedy trial and disposal of rape and offences under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012.

body.label: Operational details
body.text: It includes operationalisation of 850 Fast Track Special Courts with dedicated Judicial Officers, Special Public Prosecutors, and six support staff per court.

body.label: Funding

sections.heading: What is the Fast Track Special Courts Scheme?

body.text: The scheme, launched in 2019 and extended multiple times, was continued to strengthen judicial capacity, reduce pendency, and ensure timely justice for victims.

body.label: Major impacts

body.label: Victim-centric approach

body.label: Monitoring

sections.heading: How is the scheme implemented and monitored?

body.label: Launch and legal basis
body.text: The scheme was launched on 2 October 2019 following the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2018, and Supreme Court directions for exclusive courts in districts with over 100 pending POCSO cases.

body.label: Supreme Court directive
body.text: The Supreme Court in July 2019 mandated establishment of exclusive special courts for timely disposal of POCSO cases.

body.label: Scheme evolution
body.text: Initially for one year, the scheme has been extended several times to maintain dedicated fast track courts for sexual offence cases.

back2basics.text: Anti-bullying guidelines are rules and procedures designed to prevent and address bullying in educational institutions. back2basics.concept: Total Fertility Rate and Replacement Rate
back2basics.text: Total Fertility Rate (TFR) measures the average number of children a woman is expected to have during her lifetime. The replacement rate, usually 2.1, is the TFR at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next without migration. Falling below this rate signals a demographic shift towards an aging population and potential population decline.

2026-11-05-am-f3743800ad.deck: The Supreme Court ruled on November 4, 2026, that laws penalising having more than two children are no longer relevant due to India's declining fertility rate. This judgment has implications for population policy and constitutional rights, making it important for UPSC aspirants studying social issues and governance.

body.label: Outdated laws
body.text: The Supreme Court held that laws penalising having more than two children have lost their relevance because the fear of overpopulation has diminished due to demographic changes over the past decades.

body.label: Judgment basis
body.text: The Court noted India's Total Fertility Rate (TFR) fell from 3.02 to 1.9, below the replacement rate of 2.1, indicating a demographic transition towards an older population.

body.label: Violation of rights
body.text: The Court found that linking motherhood to political representation violates Article 21 of the Constitution, impinging on reproductive autonomy and democratic participation.

body.label: Demographic transition impact

body.label: Legal and policy implications

body.text: The judgment arose from a petition by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, whose election as Sarpanch was set aside due to having more than two children, violating the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act.

body.label: Court's interim relief
body.text: The Supreme Court allowed her to continue in office and stayed proceedings against her while calling for a larger Bench to reconsider the earlier precedent.
